x.ASV: Praise ye Jehovah. Praise ye the name of Jehovah; Praise him, O ye servants of Jehovah,

nt: The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

The psalmist is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to his reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [everything about Yahweh]

Rather he is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom the Israelites worship. See the introduction to Psalms for further discussion. Alternate translation: [the God whom we worship]

nt: Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [After all]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I know** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize how confident he is in this knowledge. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I definitely know]

The psalmist is using the phrase **from the end of the earth** as a common expression to mean “from distant places.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. The psalmist is speaking to **Egypt**, which cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about what God did there. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Egypt. Alternate translation: [right in front of the Egyptians]

nt: יְ֭הוָה שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֣ לְ⁠עוֹלָ֑ם יְ֝הוָ֗ה זִכְרְ⁠ךָ֥ לְ⁠דֹר־וָ⁠דֹֽר

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, you will be known and remembered through every generation] or [Yahweh, your name is to forever, indeed, your remembrance is to generation and generation]

Here, **name** represents Yahweh’s reputation and character. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the idea with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [your reputation]

The psalmist is using **to forever** as a common expression of his culture to mean “eternally” or “without end.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [lasts throughout eternity]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **remembrance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people will remember you from generation to generation]

The psalmist is using the phrase **to generation and generation** as a common expression to mean “forever.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is through all generations] or [is forever]
